label: ass:moments
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:moments}
Let $1\leq p<\infty$ and $\mu$ be a positive Radon measure on $X^i$ satisfying $\int_{X^i}\prod_{t=1}^i|h_t|_X^p\,d\mu(h_1,\ldots,h_i)<\infty$.
head: environment
name: Mixed moment condition

label: lem:seminorm_norm
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The bound \eqref{eq:normr_bounded_opnorm} follows from Assumption~\ref{ass:moments} and the inequality (see Proposition~\ref{lemma:multilinear}):
$$|L(h_1,\ldots,h_i)|_Y\leq\|L\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}\prod_{t=1}^i|h_t|_X.$$


{To check that $ \|\cdot\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}$ is a norm when $\operatorname{supp}\mu\supset {(S^{X,1})^i}$, it is enough to check that $\|L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}=0$ implies $L=0$. Indeed,  assume $\|L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}{=}0$. 
Denote $$g(h_1,\ldots,h_i):=|L(h_1,\ldots,h_i)|_Y^p.$$ Since $L\in \mathcal L^i(X,Y)$, $g$ is continuous and nonnegative. 
If $g(h_{0,1},\ldots,h_{0,i})>0$  at some $(h_{0,1},\ldots,h_{0,i}) \in \operatorname{supp} \mu$, continuity     would give an open neighborhood $U\subset X^i$ such that $(h_{0,1},\ldots,h_{0,i}) \in U$ and $g>g\left(h_{0,1},\ldots,h_{0,i}\right) / 2$ on $U$; by the definition of support, $\mu(U)>0$, from which $\int_{X^i} g d \mu\geq \int_U g d \mu \geq \mu(U) g\left(h_{0,1},\ldots,h_{0,i}\right) / 2$, contradicting $\int_{X^i} g d \mu=0$. Hence $$g=0,\quad \textit{on } \operatorname{supp}\mu\supset {(S^{X,1})^i},\quad \textit{i.e. }\|L\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}=0$$ Then $L=0$.}
head: environment

label: rem:target_nondegeneracy
title: Remark
head: environment

label: rem:moment_condition
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:moment_condition}
The moment condition in Assumption~\ref{ass:moments} ensures, through
\eqref{eq:normr_bounded_opnorm}, that
$\|\cdot\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}$ is finite on $\mathcal L^i(X,Y)$,
but it is not necessary for this in general. For instance, for $i=1$ and $Y=\mathbb R$, finiteness on $X^*$ is precisely
the existence of weak $p$-th moments, i.e.\
$\int_X|x^*(h)|^p\,d\mu(h)<\infty$ for every $x^*\in X^*$.
In infinite-dimensional  spaces, this condition is strictly
weaker than $\int_X|h|_X^p\,d\mu(h)<\infty$, see
\cite[Section II.2.1, Theorem 2.1]{vakhania-tarialadze}.
head: environment

label: prop:Lp_norm_separable
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
($\Rightarrow$) Let $X$ be separable and let $\{x_n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be dense in $S^{X,1}$. Set $
u:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}2^{-n}\delta_{x_n}$ and $\mu:=\otimes_{j=1}^i
u$, a Radon probability measure on $X^i$ with $\int_{X^i}\prod_{t=1}^i|h_t|_X^p\,d\mu=1$ and we have ootnote{Each point \((x_{n_1},\ldots,x_{n_i})\) belongs to \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\), since every neighborhood of it has positive \(\mu\)-measure. As the support is closed and these points are dense in \((S^{X,1})^i\), we obtain \((S^{X,1})^i\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\mu\). Conversely, \(\mu\) is concentrated on the closed set \((S^{X,1})^i\), so \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq(S^{X,1})^i\). Hence \(\operatorname{supp}\mu=(S^{X,1})^i\).} $\operatorname{supp}\mu=(S^{X,1})^i$, so that $\|\cdot\|_{L^p_{\mu}(X^i,Y)}$ is a norm by Proposition~ef{lem:seminorm_norm}. 

($\Leftarrow$) Let Assumption~ef{ass:moments} hold. Assume that $\|\cdot\|_{L^p_{\mu}(X^i,Y)}$ is a norm.  We can assume that $\mu$ is finite in view of the following. Set $w(h_1,\ldots,h_i):=\prod_{t=1}^i|h_t|_X^p$ and $d
u:= rac{w}{1+w}\,d\mu$. Then $
u$ is finite Radon and satisfies the same moment condition, since $
u(X^i)+\int_{X^i}w\,d
u=\int_{X^i}w\,d\mu<\infty$, and the corresponding seminorms have the same kernel. Thus, replacing $\mu$ by $
u$, we may assume that $\mu$ is finite. 

Being    Radon, $\mu$ is concentrated    on a $\sigma$-compact, hence separable, set $K\subset X^i$ (i.e. $\mu(X^i\setminus K)=0$, with $K= igcup_{n\in\mathbb N}K_n$ for some compact sets $K_n\subset X^i$; by tightness, one can take $K_n$ such that $\mu(X^i\setminus K_n)<1/n$),     so that $$Z:=\overline{\operatorname{span}\,\pi_1(K)}, \qquad  	extit{where } \pi_1(h_1,\ldots,h_i):=h_1,$$ is a separable       closed subspace of $X$. We show that 
$$X=Z,$$
which, in turn, implies   that $X$ is separable,     concluding the proof.
 Indeed, assume by contradiction    that $Z
eq X$. Then, by the Hahn--Banach theorem, there exists $x^*\in X^*\setminus\{0\}$ vanishing on $Z$; fixing $y_0\in Y\setminus\{0\}$, the map ootnote{the product is needed: for $i\geq2$, the map $(h_1,\ldots,h_i)\mapsto x^*(h_1)\,y_0$ is constant in $h_2,\ldots,h_i$, hence not $i$-linear} $L(h_1,\ldots,h_i):= ig(\prod_{t=1}^i x^*(h_t) ig)\,y_0$ is    nonzero    and vanishes on $K$ (since, for $(h_1,\ldots,h_i)\in K$ we have $h_1\in\pi_1(K)\subset Z$, hence $x^*(h_1)=0$, which implies that $L$ vanishes on $K$) so that $$\|L\|_{L^p_{\mu}(X^i,Y)}^p=\int_K|L(h_1,\ldots,h_i)|_Y^p\,d\mu=0,$$ contradicting     the fact that $\|\cdot\|_{L^p_{\mu}(X^i,Y)}$ is a norm. Hence $X=Z$.
head: environment

label: prop:finite-dim
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) By \eqref{eq:normr_bounded_opnorm}, the topology induced by $\|\cdot\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}$ is weaker than the one induced by $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}$.

Let $X$ be finite dimensional, and note that $\|\cdot\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,\mathbb R)}$ is a norm on the finite-dimensional space $\mathcal L^i(X,\mathbb R)$ by Remark~\ref{rem:target_nondegeneracy}; hence, by equivalence of norms in this case, there exists $C>0$ such that $\|z\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,\mathbb R)}\leq C\|z\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,\mathbb R)}$ for all $z\in\mathcal L^i(X,\mathbb R)$. Let $L\in\mathcal L^i(X,Y)$ and $h_1,\ldots,h_i\in X$ with $|h_1|_X=\cdots=|h_i|_X=1$. By the corollary of the Hahn--Banach theorem \cite[Corollary~1.4]{brezis2011}, there exists $y^*\in Y^*$ with $\|y^*\|_{Y^*}\leq1$ and $|y^*(L(h_1,\ldots,h_i))|=y:=|L(h_1,\ldots,h_i)|_Y$. Hence, applying the above equivalence of norms to $z=y^*\circ L$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
|L(h_1,\ldots,h_i)|_Y&=|(y^*\circ L)(h_1,\ldots,h_i)|\leq\|y^*\circ L\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,\mathbb R)}\leq C\|y^*\circ L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,\mathbb R)}\\
&\leq C\|y^*\|_{Y^*}\|L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\leq C\|L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}.
\end{align*}
Taking the supremum over all such $h_1,\ldots,h_i$ gives $\|L\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}\leq C\|L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}$.

Let $X$ be infinite dimensional. We construct a sequence $(L_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subset\mathcal L^i(X,Y)$ such that $\|L_n\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}=1$ for all $n\in\mathbb N$ and $\|L_n\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\to0$, which shows that the two topologies differ (making the  one from $L^p_\mu$-norm strictly weaker). Indeed, by Proposition~\ref{prop:Lp_norm_separable}, $X$ is separable; let $\{x_k\}_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be dense in $X$. For $n\in\mathbb N$, $\operatorname{span}\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\neq X$, so, by the Hahn--Banach theorem, there exists $f_n\in X^*$ with $\|f_n\|_{X^*}=1$ vanishing on $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. Fix $z^*\in X^*$ and $y_0\in Y$ with $\|z^*\|_{X^*}=|y_0|_Y=1$, and set $$L_n(h_1,\ldots,h_i):=f_n(h_1)\prod_{t=2}^iz^*(h_t)\,y_0.$$ Then:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Convergence in $L^p_\mu$.} Since $f_n(x_k)=0$ for $n\geq k$, we have $f_n(x_k)\to0$ for all $k$; since $\|f_n\|_{X^*}=1$ and $\{x_k\}$ is dense, $f_n(x)\to0$ for all $x\in X$.\footnote{Indeed, given $x\in X$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $k\in\mathbb N$ with $|x-x_k|_X<\varepsilon$; then, for all $n\geq k$, $|f_n(x)|\leq|f_n(x_k)|+|f_n(x-x_k)|\leq\|f_n\|_{X^*}|x-x_k|_X<\varepsilon$.} Hence $L_n\to0$ pointwise on $X^i$.  Since $|L_n(h_1,\ldots,h_i)|_Y^p\leq\prod_{t=1}^i|h_t|_X^p$, which is $\mu$-integrable by assumption, dominated convergence gives $\|L_n\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\to0$.
\item \emph{Operator norm.} $\|L_n\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}=\|f_n\|_{X^*}\|z^*\|_{X^*}^{i-1}|y_0|_Y=1$ for all $n\in\mathbb N$.
\end{itemize}

(ii) Let $Y$ be a Banach space and let $I\colon\big(\mathcal L^i(X,Y),\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}\big)\to\big(\mathcal L^i(X,Y),\|\cdot\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\big)$ be the identity map. By Proposition~\ref{lemma:multilinear}, $\big(\mathcal L^i(X,Y),\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}\big)$ is a Banach space, since $Y$ is; moreover, $I$ is a linear bijection, which is bounded by \eqref{eq:normr_bounded_opnorm}. If $X$ is finite dimensional, the two norms are equivalent by (i), so that $\big(\mathcal L^i(X,Y),\|\cdot\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\big)$ is complete. Conversely, assume that $\big(\mathcal L^i(X,Y),\|\cdot\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\big)$ is complete. Then both spaces are Banach spaces, so that, by the bounded inverse theorem \cite[Section~2.3]{brezis2011}, $I^{-1}$ is bounded, i.e.\ there exists $C>0$ such that
\[
\|L\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}\leq C\|L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\qquad\text{for all }L\in \mathcal L^i(X,Y).
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:normr_bounded_opnorm}, this shows that the two norms are equivalent, so that $X$ is finite dimensional by (i).
head: environment

label: prop:bounded_sets
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:bounded_sets}
Let Assumption~\ref{ass:moments} hold. Assume that $\|\cdot\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}$ is a norm on $\mathcal L^i(X,Y)$. On every operator-norm-bounded subset of $\mathcal L^i(X,Y)$, the topology induced by this norm coincides with the strong operator topology and the compact-open topology\footnote{topologies  of pointwise and uniform convergence on compact subsets of $X^i$, respectively}. In particular, all such norms, independently of the measure and the finite exponent, induce the same topology on these subsets. If $Y$ is finite dimensional, these topologies also coincide with the weak operator topology.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $Y$ is finite dimensional, the weak and norm topologies on $Y$ coincide, so that the weak and strong operator topologies coincide. By Proposition~\ref{prop:Lp_norm_separable}, $X$ is separable; fix a countable dense set $D\subset X$. Since the strong operator and compact-open topologies coincide on operator-norm-bounded subsets and are metrizable (the pointwise topology is determined by the countably many evaluations on $D^i$), it suffices to show that, for every $(L_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subset\mathcal L^i(X,Y)$ with $\sup_n\|L_n\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}<\infty$ and every $L\in\mathcal L^i(X,Y)$,
\[
\|L_n-L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\to0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L_n(h)\to L(h)\quad\text{for all }h\in X^i.
\]
Indeed, set $M:=\sup_n\|L_n-L\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}<\infty$.

($\Leftarrow$) Let $L_n\to L$ pointwise. Since\footnote{Note that, if $X$ is Banach, this implication does not require an a priori uniform bound on $\|L_n-L\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,Y)}$, since this follows from pointwise convergence by the multilinear Banach--Steinhaus theorem.} \(
|(L_n-L)(h_1,\ldots,h_i)|_Y^p\leq M^p\prod_{t=1}^i|h_t|_X^p
\), dominated convergence gives $\|L_n-L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\to0$.

($\Rightarrow$) Assume that $\|L_n-L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}\to0$. We first show that the weak$^*$ topology (hence, pointwise topology) and the scalar $L^p_\mu(X^i,\mathbb R)$-norm topologies coincide on the closed ball $\mathcal B_M$ of radius $M$ in $\mathcal L^i(X,\mathbb R)$. Indeed,
 let $E:=X^{\widehat\otimes_\pi i}$ be the completed $i$-fold projective tensor product, giving the isometric isomorphism $\mathcal L^i(X,\mathbb R)\cong E^*$ \cite[Section~2.2]{ryan2002tensor}. Thus $\mathcal B_M$, 
identifies with the closed ball of radius $M$ in $E^*$, which is weak$^*$-compact by Banach--Alaoglu. By the scalar version\footnote{Notice that the scalar seminorm is a norm by Remark~\ref{rem:target_nondegeneracy}.} of ($\Leftarrow$) and metrizability, the identity from $\mathcal B_M$ (endowed with this topology) into the scalar $L^p_\mu$-normed space is continuous. Thus this identity is a homeomorphism onto its image (i.e. a continuous bijection with continuous inverse), since its domain is compact and its target is Hausdorff\footnote{Note that this step may fail if the scalar $L^p_\mu$-seminorm (and hence the full $L^p_\mu$-seminorm) is not a norm.} \cite[Theorem~26.6]{munkres2000topology}; that is the pointwise and scalar $L^p_\mu$-norm topologies coincide on $\mathcal B_M$.

Consequently, for every $h\in X^i$ and $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that if
\(
z\in\mathcal B_M,
\|z\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,\mathbb R)}<\delta\), then  \(|z(h)|<\varepsilon.
\)
Applying this, for sufficiently large $n$ and every $y^*\in Y^*$ with $\|y^*\|_{Y^*}\leq1$, we have $\|y^*\circ(L_n-L)\|_{\mathcal L^i(X,\mathbb R)}\leq M$ and
\[
\begin{gathered}
\|y^*\circ(L_n-L)\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,\mathbb R)}
\leq\|L_n-L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}<\delta
\Longrightarrow\quad |y^*((L_n-L)(h))|<\varepsilon.
\end{gathered}
\]

By the corollary of the Hahn--Banach theorem \cite[Corollary~1.4]{brezis2011}, for each $n$ there exists $y_n^*\in Y^*$ with $\|y_n^*\|_{Y^*}\leq1$ and $|y_n^*((L_n-L)(h))|=y:=|(L_n-L)(h)|_Y$. Hence, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
|(L_n-L)(h)|_Y=y=|y_n^*((L_n-L)(h))|<\varepsilon,
\]

which proves pointwise convergence.

label: ex:discrete
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:discrete}
Let $\{x_n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence in $\{h\in X:|h|_X\leq1\}^i$ whose closure contains $(S^{X,1})^i$, and let $w_n>0$, $n\in\mathbb N$, with $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}w_n<\infty$. Then $\mu:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}w_n\delta_{x_n}$ is a finite Radon measure on $X^i$ satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:moments}, with $\operatorname{supp}\mu\supset(S^{X,1})^i$, and \eqref{norm:Lp_operators} becomes a weighted $\ell^p$-norm of the values of $L$ along $\{x_n\}$:
\[
\|L\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}=\Big(\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}w_n|L(x_n)|_Y^p\Big)^{1/p},\qquad L\in\mathcal L^i(X,Y),
\]
which is a norm by Proposition~\ref{lem:seminorm_norm}. The measure $\mu$ in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:Lp_norm_separable} is of this form. For $i=p=1$, $w_n=2^{-n}$ and $\{x_n\}$ dense in the closed unit ball of $X$, we obtain $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}2^{-n}|Lx_n|_Y$, which is classically used to metrize the strong operator topology on bounded subsets of $\mathcal L(X,Y)$, see e.g.\ \cite[Remark~3.19(d)]{kruse-schwenninger2022}.

label: ex:gaussian_measures_radonifying
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:gaussian_measures_radonifying}Let $X$, $Y$ be Banach spaces, and let $\gamma$ be a centered Gaussian
Radon measure on $X$ (for the definition, see \cite{bogachev1998gaussian}). Its RKHS $X_\gamma$ coincides with the
Cameron--Martin space (therefore,  we will use the same notation $X_\gamma$ to indicate both) and is separable. The product measure $\mu:=\otimes_{j=1}^i\gamma$ satisfies Assumption~\ref{ass:moments} with $p=2$. Then, for all $L\in\mathcal L^i(X;Y)$, we have $L_\gamma\in\gamma^i(X_\gamma,Y)$ {(recall the iterated spaces $\gamma^i(H,Y)=\gamma(H,\gamma^{i-1}(H,Y))$ from {Appendix~\ref{app:basics}})} with\footnote{If $Y$ is Hilbert, then
$\gamma^i(X_\gamma,Y)=\mathcal L_2^i(X_\gamma,Y)$ isometrically, so this
reduces to~\eqref{eq:norm2=HS}}
\[
  \|L\|_{L^2_{\otimes_{j=1}^i\gamma}(X^i,Y)}
  =\|L_\gamma\|_{\gamma^i(X_\gamma,Y)}.
\]


Indeed, let  $i=1$; define the  
 Gaussian measure $\lambda:=L_\#\gamma$ on $Y$.  Its covariance is
$R_\lambda=LR_\gamma L^*=TT^*$, where we have used that
$R_\gamma=\iota_\gamma\iota_\gamma^*$ and we have set $T:=L\iota_\gamma$. Since $\iota_\gamma \in \gamma(X_\gamma,X)$ (see \cite[Proposition 8.6]{van-neerven2010}), by \cite[Theorem 6.2]{van-neerven2010}, we have $T\in\gamma(X_\gamma,Y)$.
Thus, by  \cite[Theorem~7.4]{van-neerven2010}, we have 
\[
  \|T\|_{\gamma(X_\gamma,Y)}^2
  =\int_Y|y|_Y^2d\lambda(y)
  =\int_X|Lh|_Y^2d\gamma(h)
  =\|L\|_{L^2_\gamma(X,Y)}^2.
\]
For $i\geq2$, we proceed by induction similarly to Example \ref{ex:HS_norms_RKHS} to prove the claim.

label: eq:Phi_isometry
title: Proof
body_md:
(a) By Examples~\ref{ex:HS_norms_RKHS} and~\ref{ex:gaussian_measures_radonifying}, $\Phi:\mathcal L^i(X,Y)\to \mathcal S$, $\Phi(L):=L\circ(\iota,\ldots,\iota)$, is a linear map satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi_isometry}
\|\Phi(L)\|_{\mathcal S}=\|L\|_{L^2_\mu(X^i,Y)},\qquad L\in\mathcal L^i(X,Y).
\end{equation}
Hence $\ker\Phi=\mathcal N$ and, with $E:=\big(\mathcal L^i(X,Y)/\mathcal N,\|\cdot\|_{L^2_\mu(X^i,Y)}\big)$, the map $\tilde\Phi\colon E\to\mathcal S$, $\tilde\Phi([L]):=\Phi(L)$, is a well-defined linear isometry.  Since $\mathcal S$ is complete, $\tilde\Phi$ extends to a linear isometry  $\widehat\Phi\colon\widehat E\to\mathcal S$ on the completion $\widehat E$, whose range is
\[
\widehat\Phi(\widehat E)=\overline{\Phi(\mathcal L^i(X,Y))}^{\,\mathcal S}\subset\mathcal S.
\]

Therefore, it remains to show that $\overline{\Phi(\mathcal L^i(X,Y))}^{\,\mathcal S}\supset\mathcal S.$ To this end, let $\mathcal T:=\operatorname{span}\{h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_i\otimes y:\ h_1,\ldots,h_i\in H,\ y\in Y\}$ (recall Appendix~\ref{app:basics}). For $x_1^*,\ldots,x_i^*\in X^*$ and $y\in Y$, we have $\Phi(x_1^*\otimes\cdots\otimes x_i^*\otimes y)=\iota^*x_1^*\otimes\cdots\otimes\iota^*x_i^*\otimes y$; i.e., $\Phi(\mathcal L^i(X,Y))$ contains all $h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_i\otimes y$ with $h_1,\ldots,h_i\in\iota^*(X^*)$ and $y\in Y$. Moreover, by \eqref{eq:cross_norm} (see below) and Proposition~\ref{lemma:multilinear}, the multilinear map $(h_1,\ldots,h_i)\mapsto h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_i\otimes y$ is continuous from $H^i$ into $\mathcal S$. Since $\iota^*(X^*)$ is dense\footnote{Indeed, $\iota$ maps $\iota^*(X^*)$ onto $R(X^*)$, where $R:=\iota\iota^*$ is the covariance operator $R_\nu$, resp.\ $R_\gamma$, and $H$ is, by construction, the completion of $R(X^*)$; see Examples~\ref{ex:HS_norms_RKHS} and~\ref{ex:gaussian_measures_radonifying}.} in $H$, it follows that $h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_i\otimes y\in\overline{\Phi(\mathcal L^i(X,Y))}^{\,\mathcal S}\supset\mathcal T$ for all $h_1,\ldots,h_i\in H$ and $y\in Y$. Thus, since $\mathcal T$ is dense in $\mathcal S$ (see below), we have
\[
\overline{\Phi(\mathcal L^i(X,Y))}^{\,\mathcal S}\supset\overline{\mathcal T}^{\,\mathcal S}=\mathcal S,
\]
so that $\widehat\Phi\colon\widehat E\to\mathcal S$ is an isometric isomorphism.




It remains to verify the two facts used above, namely that $\mathcal T$ is dense in $\mathcal S$ and that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cross_norm}
\|h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_i\otimes y\|_{\mathcal S}=\prod_{t=1}^i|h_t|_H\,|y|_Y.
\end{equation}
In setting (i), write $\mathcal T_i:=\mathcal T$ and argue by induction on $i$, with $\mathcal L_2^0(H,Y):=Y$ and $\mathcal T_0:=Y$. Set $Z:=\mathcal L_2^{i-1}(H,Y)$, so that $\mathcal L_2^i(H,Y)=\mathcal L_2(H,Z)$ (see Appendix~\ref{app:basics}). For $h\in H$ and $z\in Z$, choosing an orthonormal basis $\{e_n\}$ of $H$, Parseval's identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank_one_HS}
\|h\otimes z\|_{\mathcal L_2(H,Z)}^2=\sum_n\|(h\otimes z)e_n\|_Z^2=\sum_n|\langle e_n,h\rangle_H|^2\,\|z\|_Z^2=|h|_H^2\,\|z\|_Z^2.
\end{equation}
For $i=1$, i.e.\ $Z=Y$, this is \eqref{eq:cross_norm}; for $i\geq2$, applying \eqref{eq:rank_one_HS} with $h=h_1$ and $z=h_2\otimes\cdots\otimes h_i\otimes y\in Z$, and using \eqref{eq:cross_norm} for $i-1$, we obtain \eqref{eq:cross_norm} for $i$:
\[
\|h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_i\otimes y\|_{\mathcal L_2^i(H,Y)}=\|h_1\otimes(h_2\otimes\cdots\otimes h_i\otimes y)\|_{\mathcal L_2(H,Z)}=|h_1|_H\,\|h_2\otimes\cdots\otimes h_i\otimes y\|_{Z}=\prod_{t=1}^i|h_t|_H\,|y|_Y.
\]
Similarly, for $i=1$, $\mathcal T_1=H\otimes Y$ is the space of finite-rank operators from $H$ to $Y$, which is dense in $\mathcal L_2(H,Y)$. Next, let $i\geq2$ and assume that $\mathcal T_{i-1}$ is dense in $Z$. Given $A\in\mathcal L_2(H,Z)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, since the space of finite-rank operators $H\otimes Z$ is dense in $\mathcal L_2(H,Z)$, we can choose $\sum_{k=1}^m h_k\otimes z_k\in H\otimes Z$ with $\|A-\sum_{k=1}^m h_k\otimes z_k\|_{\mathcal L_2(H,Z)}<\varepsilon$ and, by the induction hypothesis, $z_k'\in\mathcal T_{i-1}$ with $|h_k|_H\|z_k-z_k'\|_Z<\varepsilon/m$. Then $\sum_{k=1}^m h_k\otimes z_k'\in H\otimes\mathcal T_{i-1}\subset\mathcal T_i$ and, by the triangle inequality and \eqref{eq:rank_one_HS},
\begin{align*}
\Big\|A-\sum_{k=1}^m h_k\otimes z_k'\Big\|_{\mathcal L_2(H,Z)}
&\leq\Big\|A-\sum_{k=1}^m h_k\otimes z_k\Big\|_{\mathcal L_2(H,Z)}+\sum_{k=1}^m\big\|h_k\otimes(z_k-z_k')\big\|_{\mathcal L_2(H,Z)}\\
&<\varepsilon+\sum_{k=1}^m|h_k|_H\|z_k-z_k'\|_Z<2\varepsilon,
\end{align*} 
which proves the density of $\mathcal T_i$ in $\mathcal L_2^i(H,Y)$.

In setting (ii), the same argument applies with $\mathcal L_2$ replaced by $\gamma$ (and $\gamma^0(H,Y):=Y$), since $\gamma^i(H,Y)=\gamma(H,\gamma^{i-1}(H,Y))$ (see Appendix~\ref{app:basics}) and since, by definition of $\gamma(H,Z)$, $H\otimes Z$ is dense in $\gamma(H,Z)$ and $\|h\otimes z\|_{\gamma(H,Z)}=|h|_H\|z\|_Z$ for $h\in H$ and $z\in Z$.




(b) Set $V:=\overline{\iota(H)}$. By \eqref{eq:Phi_isometry} and the injectivity of $\mathcal S\hookrightarrow\mathcal L^i(H,Y)$ (recall Appendix~\ref{app:basics}), $L\in\mathcal N$ if and only if $L$ vanishes on $\iota(H)^i$, or, by continuity, on $V^i$. If $V=X$, then $\mathcal N=\{0\}$. If $V\neq X$ and $Y\neq\{0\}$, choose $x^*\in X^*\setminus\{0\}$ vanishing on $V$ by the Hahn--Banach theorem, and $y_0\in Y\setminus\{0\}$. Then $x^*\otimes\cdots\otimes x^*\otimes y_0$ is a nonzero element of $\mathcal N$.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:gaussian_finite_p}
In the Gaussian setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:completion}(ii), the seminorms $\|\cdot\|_{L^p_\mu(X^i,Y)}$, $1\leq p<\infty$, are equivalent, with constants depending only on $i$ and the exponents \cite[Proposition~3.1]{maas2010} (see also \cite[Proposition~2.7(2)]{van-neerven2010}).  For every $1\leq p<\infty$, the restriction map in Theorem~\ref{thm:completion}(a) therefore extends to an isomorphism from the $L^p_\mu$-completion of $\mathcal L^i(X,Y)/\mathcal N$ onto $\gamma^i(X_\gamma,Y)$, with equivalent norms.

name: Other finite exponents

label: rem:completion_unbounded
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:completion_unbounded}
In the setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:completion}, assume that $\mathcal N=\{0\}$ and that $X$ is infinite dimensional. By Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-dim}(ii), $\mathcal S$ contains elements $T$ whose pullbacks $T\circ(\iota^{-1},\ldots,\iota^{-1})$ are unbounded with respect to $|\cdot|_X$ and therefore admit no bounded multilinear extension to $X^i$. For instance, for centered Gaussian $\gamma$, $i=1$ and $Y=\mathbb R$, this corresponds to the classical fact that $\overline{X^*}^{\,L^2(X;\gamma)}$, identified with $(X_\gamma)^*$, consists  of (equivalence classes of) $\gamma$-measurable linear functionals, which need not admit continuous representatives on $X$ \cite[Theorems~2.10.9, 2.10.11]{bogachev1998gaussian}.
